title: Battery recoverability (V720–V724)
dek: NASA PCoE LCO relaxation trajectories: active restoration-deficit beats passive snap distance — an applied recoverability assay.

notes.title: NASA battery assay and Tesla letter

claims.text: On this public NASA dataset and the published synthetics, active restoration-deficit scoring outperforms passive snap. This is an applied recoverability result. It does not solve battery aging and does not derive field equations.

text:
The retained-atlas framework was pressure-tested on the NASA PCoE LCO battery dataset (V720) and on synthetic assays V723/V724. Passive “snap distance” (instantaneous voltage drop) delivers AUC 0.6366 and is already collapsing toward chance. Integrated restoration-deficit metrics — early_auc, tail_auc, full_auc — reach AUC 0.9326 and Spearman 0.8715 to capacity loss. Residualizing out the initial snap still leaves AUC 0.8655.

V723 holds passive burden metrics at chance (~0.500) while active adm_z separates perfectly (AUC 1.000) in the synthetic. V724 adds overlapping k, nonlinear saturation, reserve fatigue, stochastic stalls, and shortened windows; signal holds at ≈0.845. Geometry-like structures (curvature concentration, geodesic relaxation, stress localization) are reported as emergent in the assay, not imposed.

On this public NASA dataset and the published synthetics, active restoration-deficit scoring outperforms passive snap. This is an applied recoverability result. It does not solve battery aging and does not derive field equations.

A 18 May 2026 open letter (posted from the account, attributed as a Grok draft) argued Tesla already collects the relevant rest-window voltages in BMS health checks. That is advocacy built on the assay, not a Tesla collaboration claim. The original V723/V724 assay video is 18 May: passive burden held equivalent, active perturbation-response still showing restorative structure — observation only, synthetic, falsifiable.
